candidates.attacker_control: Unauthenticated HTTP GET path variables of the default resource endpoints `/{name}/{profile}/{label}/**` (and the octet-stream variant at ResourceController.java:132-144): name, profile, label and the remaining path are fully attacker-controlled, and the config server normally has no authentication configured (Spring Security is optional). The label is attacker-controlled text; `(_)` is accepted literally in a path segment.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Path-level traversal is defended: GenericResourceRepository rejects `..` in the trailing path (isInvalidPath, lines 211-236) and re-checks single-encoded forms (isInvalidEncodedPath, lines 116-135), so the classic `/{name}/{profile}/{label}/..%2f..` payload is blocked. The issue therefore depends on the label/location vector, which has no equivalent check anywhere in ResourceController, NativeEnvironmentRepository.getLocations, or GenericResourceRepository.findOne. classpath: search locations are not escapable the same way (ClassPathResource relative resolution does not resolve `..` on the filesystem), so the file: locations are the exploitable ones. I did not find any other validation of the resolved label (no assert/pattern check) in the reviewed sources.
candidates.impact: Disclosure of arbitrary files readable by the config server process that can be reached by `..` from a configured file:-based search location (e.g. /etc/passwd, secrets or config-adjacent files under the deployment directory); no write or code execution. On typical deployments the native profile plus default file:./ locations makes this reachable without special configuration.
candidates.prerequisites: Config server running with the native environment repository active (e.g. spring.profiles.active=native) and the default `spring.cloud.config.server.native.add-label-locations=true` (NativeEnvironmentProperties.java:34-40); a file:-based (or otherwise filesystem-backed) search location such as the defaults `file:./`, `file:./config/` (NativeEnvironmentRepository.java:59-60); attacker can recurse upward with enough `..` segments and knows/guesses a readable target filename in the escaped directory (the trailing path component itself must not contain `..`, since that part is checked).
candidates.root_cause: ResourceController.resolveLabel() rewrites the attacker-supplied label from `(_)` to `/` (ResourceController.java:189-196) and passes that resolved label to the ResourceRepository (ResourceController.java:103-107). NativeEnvironmentRepository.getLocations() then builds location strings as `location + label.trim() + "/"` when addLabelLocations is true (NativeEnvironmentRepository.java:194-203); `isDirectory()` is a purely syntactic check (NativeEnvironmentRepository.java:311-314) that neither resolves `..` nor confines the result to the configured root, so it adds a location such as `file:./../../../etc/`. GenericResourceRepository.findOne() uses those location strings directly in `resourceLoader.getResource(location).createRelative(local)` (GenericResourceRepository.java:60-76) while validating only the trailing `local` path via isInvalidPath/isInvalidEncodedPath (GenericResourceRepository.java:211-236); a harmless trailing name without `..` (e.g. `passwd`) passes, and the OS resolves the `..` already embedded in the location.
candidates.title: ResourceController label → native search-location traversal allows reading files outside configured search locations
candidates.trace: Request `/app/prod/..(_)..(_)..(_)etc/passwd` → Spring MVC binds name=app, profile=prod, label=`..(_)..(_)..(_)etc`, path=`passwd`; ResourceController.getFilePath uses the raw label so `path` becomes `passwd` (ResourceController.java:89-101); retrieve() then calls resolveLabel(), turning the label into `../../../etc` (ResourceController.java:105-107), and invokes resourceRepository.findOne("app","prod","../../../etc","passwd") (ResourceController.java:107). GenericResourceRepository.findOne calls service.getLocations(...) (line 64); NativeEnvironmentRepository appends the resolved label to each search location, producing e.g. `file:./../../../etc/` and adding it because isDirectory() only checks string shape (lines 194-203, 311-314). For local=`passwd`, isInvalidPath/isInvalidEncodedPath return false (lines 70, 211-236), so `file:./config/../../../etc/passwd` is resolved and, if it exists and is readable, returned to the controller and streamed to the caller (ResourceController.java:113-120).
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-confirmed: I did not execute the server or payload. It remains unverified whether Spring MVC/AntPathMatcher binds `..(_)..(_)..(_)etc` as a single {label} segment (the mapping itself permits slashes in branch names only via `(_)`, per the in-code comment), whether the servlet container leaves parentheses untouched in the lookup path, and whether UrlPathHelper/FileUrlResource relative resolution applies exactly as traced on the target platform. Which CVE (if any) this corresponds to was not checked; the snapshot has no tests to corroborate behavior.
candidates.weakness_type: Path traversal (CWE-22) via unvalidated label incorporated into repository search locations

coverage_summary: Reviewed the 160-file snapshot (137 Java files in modules: spring-cloud-config-server, -client, -monitor, -sample, -starter). Focused on the HTTP-facing server code: ResourceController/GenericResourceRepository, EnvironmentController, Native/JGit/MultipleJGit/Vault/Passthru/Svn/Jdbc/Credhub environment repositories, encryption controllers, support/ssh helpers, monitor notification endpoint, and configuration classes. P1 relation index reported partial coverage: 157 of 160 files indexed, 3 source files missing from index, 1839 unresolved calls, and no control-flow/data-flow/semantic resolution; it was used only for navigation and all conclusions were verified in source text. No tests are present in the snapshot and no build/scan was run.
limitations: No runtime execution, tests, or dependency resolution: reachability of the traced request path through Spring MVC/UrlPathHelper/FileUrlResource was reasoned from source only.
Native/Credhub/Vault/JDBC/Svn repositories were read but not exhaustively audited for secondary sinks; the client and monitor modules received lighter review.
The P1 index cannot prove data flow or exploitability and omits 3 files; findings were verified manually against source text.
No CVE/CWE ground-truth data was consulted, so the candidate is a lead, not a confirmed vulnerability.

rejected_leads.lead: Direct `..`/double-encoded path traversal through `/{name}/{profile}/{label}/**` in GenericResourceRepository
rejected_leads.reason: The CVE-2019-3799-era defenses are present: isInvalidPath plus isInvalidEncodedPath with processPath/cleanPath (GenericResourceRepository.java:116-135, 211-236) reject `..` and single-encoded forms in the trailing path; no bypass with plain or double encoding is evident from source.

rejected_leads.lead: EnvironmentController `(_)` → `/` substitution for name/label used by native/JGit repositories
rejected_leads.reason: Same substitution exists (EnvironmentController.java:111-119) but these endpoints return parsed property sources rather than raw files; I could not trace a concrete arbitrary-file-read effect as strong as the ResourceController vector, so it was not selected.

rejected_leads.lead: Vault/Credhub/proxy RestTemplate paths as potential SSRF
rejected_leads.reason: Vault host/scheme/port come from server configuration, not request input; the request token header is only forwarded as a header (HttpRequestConfigTokenProvider). No attacker-controlled URL construction was confirmed.

rejected_leads.lead: JGit label handling (checkout/fetch with attacker label)
rejected_leads.reason: Labels reach JGit ref APIs, not a shell; no argument-injection or path-escape sink was identified in source, and refresh() maps errors to NoSuchLabelException.

summary: Spring Cloud Config 2.1.6.RELEASE snapshot (server/client/monitor modules). Strongest source-evidenced issue: the ResourceController label path variable can be transformed from `(_)`-encoded form into slash-containing `../..` sequences and then concatenated into native search-location strings without any confinement check; the only traversal guards apply to the trailing resource path, not to the derived location, so `file:` locations can be escaped and arbitrary readable files served. This resembles the known label/location traversal class in spring-cloud-config (pre-2.1.9), but no CVE attribution is claimed and no runtime verification was performed. Everything else reviewed appeared adequately guarded or lacked a concrete attacker-controlled file/privilege operation.
